div.div: CPU Kernel vs Kubernetes Request and Limits

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 438px; height: 1px; padding-top: 170px; margin-left: 431px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;

div.div: The Linux Kernel is the Enforcer, but Kubernetes is the Policy Maker that tells the enforcer who is important.

div.div: The Linux Kernel has no idea what a "Kubernetes Pod" or "100m CPU" is

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.div: Kernel only understands Control Groups (cgroups) and CPU Shares.

div.div: In Kubernetes (The policy maker): You write cpu: 250m in your YAML.

div.div: he Handshake: The Kubelet takes that number and translates it for the Kernel.

div.div: The Linux Kernel (The Enforcer): It sets a value in a file called cpu.shares. By default, 1000m (1 core) = 1024 shares.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 258px; height: 1px; padding-top: 350px; margin-left: 1631px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: If Node is Idle. If your pod has a request of 100m but it’s the only thing running, the Kernel lets it use 100% of the CPU. The "request" doesn't act as a cage here.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 258px; height: 1px; padding-top: 470px; margin-left: 1641px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: If Node is Exploding (Contention). If five pods all want 100% of the CPU at the same time, the Kernel looks at the cpu.shares.

div.div: If Pod A has 1000m (1024 shares) and Pod B has 100m (102 shares), the Kernel will ensure Pod A gets 10x more time than Pod B.

path.style: stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));
fill: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.div: There is one thing the Linux Kernel cannot do: it can't prevent a node from getting too crowded. This is the primary job of Kubernetes.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 428px; height: 1px; padding-top: 510px; margin-left: 991px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: Admission Control: When you set a request, the Kubernetes Scheduler uses it as a "reservation." If a node has 4 cores and you've already scheduled pods requesting 3.8 cores, the Scheduler will refuse to put any more pods there.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(#ffffff, var(--ge-dark-color, #121212)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 438px; height: 1px; padding-top: 620px; margin-left: 991px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: The Consequence: If you didn't set requests, the Scheduler might pack 100 pods onto a single node. The Linux Kernel would try its best to be "fair," but each pod would only get 1% of the CPU, causing your entire application to crawl.
